content: Medscape AI News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More Video Events Specialties Topics RegisterLog In Medscape News UK Medbrief Human Papillomavirus Vaccination Not Tied to Early Pregnancy Complications Edited by Vinod Rane, BS Pharm August 25, 2026 0 TOPLINE A long follow-up study showed that, among women, human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination during early adolescence or as cross-vaccination during late adolescence was not associated with an increased risk for miscarriages or other adverse early pregnancy outcomes. METHODOLOGY Using data from nationwide Finnish registries, researchers conducted a longitudinal cohort study to compare the incidence of miscarriages or other abnormal early pregnancy outcomes between women with HPV vaccination and those without vaccination. The study included 20,426 women born between 1992 and 1995 who participated in a community-randomised HPV vaccination trial across 33 municipalities in 2007; 19,473 age- and community-aligned unvaccinated women born in 1990-1991 were also included as control participants. During the vaccination trial, participants received either the HPV vaccine or hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccine at ages of 12-15 years, and some participants who initially received the HBV vaccine later underwent HPV cross-vaccination at the age of 18.5 years and were considered "cross-vaccinated." Participants were followed up for 11 years. TAKEAWAY A miscarriage occurred in 1.6% of HPV-vaccinated women and 1.3% of cross-vaccinated women, compared with 5.3% of unvaccinated women, with a significant difference observed between cross-vaccinated and unvaccinated women (P < .0001). Miscarriage rates were highest among women aged 25-27 years, ranging from seven to eight per 10,000 person-years in the vaccinated group vs 14 per 10,000 person-years in the unvaccinated group. No miscarriages were reported within the first 6 years after HPV or HBV vaccination at ages of 12-15 years. Among those who underwent cross-vaccination at the age of 18.5 years, four miscarriages were reported within 24 months, none of which occurred during the first 6 months. Ectopic pregnancy rates remained low and comparable across all cohorts, ranging from 0.6% to 1.0%. Among women with a history of abnormal pregnancy outcomes, live birth rates were 55.6% for HPV-vaccinated women and 70.3% for unvaccinated women. IN PRACTICE "[The study] findings provide further reassurance on the reproductive safety of HPV vaccination, both when administered in early adolescence and as cross-vaccination in late adolescence," the authors wrote. "Continued surveillance and future studies incorporating detailed lifestyle and clinical data will help further refine our understanding of HPV vaccination and reproductive health outcomes," they added. SOURCE This study was led by Tiina Koivisto, Faculty of Medicine and Health Technology, Tampere University, Tampere, Finland. It was published online on August 12, 2026, in the European Journal of Public Health. LIMITATIONS Women who participated in the HPV vaccination trial may have differed from the unvaccinated cohort in health awareness, lifestyle habits, or other characteristics, introducing potential selection bias. The registry lacked data on lifestyle factors such as smoking, alcohol use, BMI, and contraceptive use. DISCLOSURES The study received partial support from state funding for university-level health research and Tampere University Hospital, Wellbeing Services County of Pirkanmaa, and others. One author declared receiving grants for his vaccination studies from Merck & Co., Inc. and GSK Biologicals. Read more This article was originally published by The Conversation in June 2025, and is being republished by the Independent after it was announced that women in England will receive home cervical screening kits for HPV. Few viruses are as widespread – and sometimes misunderstood – as the human papillomavirus, or HPV. It’s so common that most of us – up to 80% – will encounter it at some point in our lives, often without even realising it. Understanding HPV matters, given that it is linked to several types of cancer. Scientists have identified more than 200 types of HPV, making it one of the most diverse viral families known – and a complex one at that. Many strains are low risk, causing either no symptoms or benign warts. HPV types 1, 2 and 4, for instance, are responsible for the common skin wart. Many will have experienced these, including the familiar verruca (plantar wart) picked up at swimming pools. Some strains, such as HPV 6 and 11, cause genital warts – small growths that appear on the genitals or around the anus. Treatments such as creams, surgical removal or freezing can get rid of the visible warts, but they don’t remove the virus itself. This means the virus can still be passed to sexual partners until the body’s immune system clears it. open image in gallery HPV is a DNA virus from the papillomavirus family ( Alamy/PA ) Most seriously, certain types of HPV – particularly 16 and 18 – have known links to cancer. They belong to a group of about 14 high-risk strains that can enter human cells and damage their DNA. This damage interferes with the cells’ normal controls on growth and division, which can lead to the development of cancer. Repeated or persistent infection with these strains increases the risk of developing cancer. So, too, does smoking, which reduces the ability of the immune system to clear the virus. Because HPV comes in so many forms – from harmless skin warts to strains linked with cancer – it’s easy to see how myths and confusion can take hold. To separate fact from fiction, here are five key points that everyone should know about the virus. 1. HPV is not just associated with cervical cancer While cervical cancer remains the most recognised HPV-related malignancy, the virus is also linked to cancers of the vulva, vagina, anus, penis, mouth and throat. Emerging evidence suggests some types may also contribute to developing skin cancer. This broad cancer risk explains why the widely available HPV vaccine is recommended for both sexes. The vaccine’s ability to prevent HPV infection makes population-wide immunisation beneficial, as transmission may occur between heterosexual and homosexual partners alike. 2. You don’t need to have symptoms or genital warts to pass the virus on HPV can remain on the skin for months before the immune system clears it, allowing transmission through contact even before genital warts appear and after they’ve been treated. This is why condoms should be used for at least three months after visible warts have resolved. 3. HPV transmission can occur from more than just vaginal or anal sex Oral and throat cancers can develop following HPV infection acquired through oral sex. The incidence of mouth and throat cancer is increasing worldwide, with oral sex now the most significant behavioural risk factor. Using condoms during oral sex can help reduce this risk. About the author Dan Baumgardt is a Senior Lecturer in the School of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of Bristol. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article. HPV can also spread through the use of sex toys. One study highlighted the ability of transmissible HPV to remain on sex toys and the need to develop proper hygiene practices for cleaning, and avoiding shared use. 4. Condoms are not 100% effective at preventing spread Condoms can lower the risk of HPV transmission, but they can’t offer full protection, as uncovered skin can still carry the virus. This is why many sexually active people will come into contact with a strain of the virus at some point in their lives, even when practising safe sex. 5. Even vaccinated women need to have smear tests Current HPV vaccines target the main high-risk virus types but cannot cover all cancer-causing strains, or treat existing infections. In rarer cases, cervical cancer can also arise without HPV infection. This is why women aged 25 to 64 are still invited for cervical screening every five years, even after vaccination. Women should also seek urgent medical review for other indicators of cervical cancer. These include pain or bleeding after sex, bleeding between periods or after menopause, and changes in vaginal discharge. open image in gallery A nurse injects a dose of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine ( AFP/Getty ) Even though the HPV vaccine is widely available, uptake has dropped in some areas. The COVID pandemic disrupted routine vaccination programmes, while misinformation about the vaccine’s safety and effectiveness has shaken trust. In some places, low awareness of HPV’s link to different cancers – and of the need to vaccinate boys as well as girls – has also made public understanding more difficult. The World Health Organisation has set a target of fully vaccinating 90% of girls by age 15 by 2030. At present, only about 48% of girls worldwide are fully vaccinated, so there is more work to be done. Although HPV is often harmless, the potential consequences of some strains are too significant to ignore. But no one should be fearful of an active sex life. For those eligible for the HPV vaccine, protection is not just for the individual, but also for future sexual partners who could otherwise be exposed. By staying informed and taking preventative measures, we can reduce the effects of this common virus and keep ourselves and others safer

The scheme offers a "discreet and convenient option" intended to persuade more women to undertake screening as almost a third of women are overdue for their appointment for life-saving cervical cancer screening – due to embarrassment, discomfort or simply not having enough time to attend. Over the next year, nearly four million will receive invites to receive a free testing kit. But who is eligible and how do the at-home tests work? open image in gallery Women who are not up to date with cervical cancer screening are to be offered at-home tests to drive down cases of cervical cancer (Alamy/PA) How will the tests work? Included in each kit is a swab, which is used to collect a vaginal sample. RECOMMENDED Dolly Parton net worth: The country legend had no kids. Where is her fortune going? Where high-risk HPV is found, patients will subsequently be requested to go to a clinician for a cervical screening appointment. Normally, cervical screening is a ten minute appointment where a nurse or doctor will use a soft brush to collect a small sample of cells from your cervix. This sample is then sent to test for HPV and if the virus is found the sample is checked for any changes in the cells of your cervix. These can be treated to help prevent cervical cancer. What is HPV? HPV is a group of viruses which can be passed on through sexual contact. Some of these viruses can cause warts, some cause no symptoms at all and others increase the risk of cervical cancer. Approximately 13 high-risk forms of the virus are known to cause 99.7 per cent of all cervical cancer cases. There are around 3,300 new cases of cervical cancer every year, but rates of the disease have decreased by a quarter since the early 1990s. About 70 per cent of cases are prevented through cervical screening, according to cancer research, and the HPV vaccine is cutting cases of cervical cancer by 90 per cent. Women aged between 24 and 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years, or more often if HPV is detected. open image in gallery Approximately 13 high-risk forms of HPV are known to cause 99.7 per cent of all cervical cancer cases (Getty/iStock) Who can get the free tests? Women who have missed their cervical screening appointments will be offered the free at-home testing kits. Invitations have already started to be distributed to eligible women aged 30 to 65 who have missed appointments, arriving by letter, email, text message or the NHS app. They will then be able to order a kit through the NHS app or online. The programme specifically targets those groups consistently missing vital appointments, with younger women, ethnic minority communities facing cultural hurdles, people with a disability and LGBT+ people all set to benefit. What makes these tests a ‘game-changer’? Not all women attend screening appointments for reasons including fear of pain, concerns about privacy and stigma, and lack of awareness. Latest figures from NHS England show 68.8 per cent of eligible women are up to date with cervical screening, below the 80 per cent target. This is dangerous because cervical cancer often doesn't cause any symptoms until the disease is more advanced and harder to treat. Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women’s health at NHS England, said: “Screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier, but only around two thirds of women are attending cervical screening appointments when invited by the NHS. “Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a gamechanger – making it easier than ever for them to get tested for HPV.” Offering women an at-home self-test could prevent as many as 1,000 cases of cervical cancer every year, a study led by Queen Mary University of London with King’s College London found. More than 3,000 women are diagnosed with cervical cancer each year in the UK. It has been estimated that the number would be 5,000 higher if it weren’t for cervical screening. But at-home testing could save even more lives. MILLIONS of women in the UK will now have easy access to cervical cancer screening as the NHS rolls out new at home testing kits. The new scheme, which will provide free testing kits to women who have missed cervical cancer screening appointments at their local health centres, comes as concerns that only two-thirds of women attend these in person tests when invited. Helping to Reach 4 Million MissingnWomen Currently, all people with a cervix in the UK are offered an in-person test for human papillomavirus (HPV) on the NHS every five years between the ages of 25 and 65. However, is it estimated that around 4 million women are not up to date with their screenings. Now, women who have not attended their appointments will be eligible to order a free at-home self-test kit through the NHS app or website which will then be delivered to their door. Each kit will include a swab to collect a sample from the vagina, which can then be sent back to the NHS via free post where it will be tested in laboratories for high-risk strains of HPV. If a high-risk type of HPV is detected, patients will then be notified and asked to attend an in-person screening appointment with a clinician. These new tests will be available to all women between 30 and 65 who have not previously attended their screening appointments and eligible patients will be notified via the NHS app, text message, email or letter. Screening Saves Lives The scheme is part of the NHS’s target of eliminating cervical cancer by 2040, 99.7% types of which are caused by around just 13 strains of high-risk HPV. Officials hope that the do-it-yourself nature of the test, which can be carried out independently and privately, will encourage women who were otherwise missing their screenings to begin testing. Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women’s health at NHS England, said: “Screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier, but only around two-thirds of women are attending cervical screening appointments when invited by the NHS. “Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a gamechanger – making it easier than ever for them to get tested for HPV,” she added. NewsClinical Diagnostics Seegene announces comprehensive PCR-based reproductive tract infection testing strategy Seegene Inc Seegene promotes comprehensive HPV and STI PCR testing through the Global Million Clinical Study (GMCS) to advance reproductive tract infection diagnostics 24 Aug 2026 Seegene Inc. has announced a comprehensive syndromic PCR-based testing approach for reproductive tract infections (RTIs), combining simultaneous detection of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and human papillomavirus (HPV). Based on approximately 60,000 co-testing results analyzed over 42 months using its STAgoraTM real-time test data analytics and statistical platform, Seegene aims to validate this integrated HPV and STI testing strategy through the Global Million Clinical Study (GMCS) to establish scientific evidence for new global standards of PCR testing. Emerging evidence linking HPV, STIs and vaginal microbiome changes Analysis of approximately 60,000 HPV and STI co-testing results generated over a 42-month period Recent studies have suggested that STIs and vaginal dysbiosis may be associated with changes in the local inflammatory, immune and microbial environment of the cervix. These changes may influence HPV acquisition, persistence or clearance. This growing body of evidence underscores the importance of interpreting HPV and STI findings within the broader clinical context, including the patient’s age, symptoms, sexual history and exposure risk, pregnancy plan, prior infection history and the specific organism detected. Together, these findings provide a scientific rationale for further evaluating a comprehensive HPV and STI testing approach that assesses HPV risk alongside concurrent sexually transmitted and reproductive tract infections. By integrating pathogen detection with clinical context, laboratories and clinicians may be better equipped to stratify risk, tailor follow-up strategies and support reproductive health. STAgora analysis of 60,000 HPV and STI co-testing results Using STAgoraTM, Seegene’s real-time test data analytics and statistical platform, the company internally analyzed approximately 60,000 HPV and STI co-testing results generated over a 42‐month period. The analysis showed that: STI pathogens were detected in 82% of HPV-positive cases HPV was detected in 46% of STI-positive cases Co-detection of HPV and STI pathogens was observed in 71% of positive cases identified through comprehensive HPV and STI testing These data highlight the frequent co-occurrence of HPV and STI pathogens in reproductive tract infections and support the potential value of concurrent testing. The findings suggest that a significant proportion of individuals with HPV may also harbor one or more STI pathogens, and vice versa, reinforcing the need for integrated diagnostic strategies. Potential clinical applications of comprehensive HPV and STI testing The findings from the STAgora analysis demonstrate the potential application of concurrent STI testing with HPV screening in a range of clinical scenarios. Promising applications may include: Identifying asymptomatic STIs in individuals undergoing HPV screening Assessing co-infections in HPV-positive individuals to inform risk assessment and follow-up Supporting reproductive health evaluations during pregnancy planning or infertility assessment By providing both HPV genotype information and detailed STI pathogen profiles, comprehensive PCR-based testing may help clinicians better understand the overall reproductive tract infection status, guide appropriate treatment and counseling, and support long-term reproductive health outcomes. Global Million Clinical Study to validate comprehensive PCR testing approach The announcement of Seegene’s comprehensive RTI testing strategy follows the launch of the Global Million Clinical Study on July 8. This initiative aims to generate scientific evidence for a Global New Standard of PCR testing by accumulating real-world clinical data from healthcare institutions worldwide and evaluating the clinical utility of disease-specific diagnostic testing strategies. Through GMCS, Seegene plans to continue accumulating clinical evidence on comprehensive HPV and STI testing and to statistically evaluate its clinical utility and applicability using STAgora. By leveraging large-scale, real-world data, the company seeks to establish robust scientific evidence to support new global standards for PCR-based reproductive tract infection diagnostics. STI test target analytes in comprehensive RTI panels Seegene’s comprehensive reproductive tract infection testing approach targets a broad range of STI and related pathogens, including: Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG) Mycoplasma genitalium (MG) Trichomonas vaginalis (TV) Mycoplasma hominis (MH) Ureaplasma urealyticum (UU) Ureaplasma parvum (UP) Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) Treponema pallidum (TP) Gardnerella vaginalis (GV) Candida albicans (CA) By including these analytes alongside HPV genotyping in a single PCR-based testing strategy, laboratories can obtain a comprehensive view of reproductive tract infections that may influence cervical health, fertility and overall reproductive outcomes. content_title: Millions of women can now take a cervical screening test at home – here's how it works
content: Hands up if you've ever put off booking – or going to – your cervical screening because you felt a) embarrassed, b) worried it would hurt, c) too busy or d) you simply couldn't get an appointment. You're far from alone. Around a third of eligible women in England are currently behind on routine cervical screening, with the latest figures showing that just 68.8% are up to date – below NHS England's target of 80%. Now, in a major change to the screening programme, the NHS has started offering free HPV self-testing kits to women who haven't attended cervical screening after receiving previous invitations. The kits can be completed privately at home and posted back to an NHS laboratory, with the hope that they will remove some of the barriers that stop women from attending screening in person. ‘There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time, or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test,’ says Dr Sue Mann, National Clinical Director for Women’s Health at NHS England. So, who can get one, how does the test work and what happens if HPV is detected? Here's what you need to know. What to Read Next Who is eligible for an at-home HPV test? The rollout is initially targeting women aged 30–65 who are overdue for cervical screening or have not attended after previous invitations. A few things worth knowing: - The scheme is being introduced in phases across England - It is currently invitation-only - Invitations will arrive through the NHS App, text, email or letter - Once invited, you can order a free kit through the NHS App or your NHS online account - If you haven't been invited, you can still book a conventional cervical screening appointment through your GP or sexual health clinic The rollout forms part of the NHS's ambition to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040. How does the at-home HPV test work? The process is designed to be straightforward and doesn't require a GP appointment or another person to take the sample. The kit contains a swab – similar to a long cotton bud – which you use to collect a sample from the vagina. You then post it back to an NHS laboratory using the free return system. The sample is checked for high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV). According to the NHS, HPV is a common group of viruses that can be passed on through sexual contact and usually causes no symptoms. There are more than 200 different types. Some are considered low-risk, while others are classed as high-risk because they can cause cell changes that may eventually lead to cervical cancer. What happens if HPV is detected? First things first: a positive HPV result does not mean you have cervical cancer. ‘High-risk HPV may cause cervical cell changes. These cells aren’t cancer but could lead to cervical cancer in the future if they are not monitored or treated,’ explains Helen Hyndman, MBE, Lead Nurse at The Eve Appeal. If high-risk HPV is detected, you'll be invited to a follow-up cervical screening appointment with a nurse or doctor. ‘This is so that the healthcare professional can get a sample from your cervix which can be checked for high-risk HPV and changes to the cells of your cervix,’ says Hyndman. If HPV is present but there are no abnormal cell changes, you may be invited for another screening test at a later date. If abnormal changes are found, you may be referred for a colposcopy, where a specialist examines the cervix more closely. The important thing to remember is that cervical screening is designed to identify risk early, before cell changes have the chance to develop into cancer. Is the home test replacing cervical screening? No. Cervical screening appointments carried out by a clinician remain the standard route for women who already attend their appointments, and the NHS is clear that those who routinely go for screening should continue to do so. The self-test is being introduced as an additional option for people who haven't taken up previous invitations. Dr Mann has described the rollout as a ‘gamechanger’ for women who have struggled to attend conventional screening. Athena Lamnisos, CEO of gynaecological cancer charity The Eve Appeal, agrees that self-testing could remove significant barriers, while stressing the importance of continuing to improve traditional screening too. ‘This is not a replacement for clinician screening, and we will continue to work with and support those attending their traditional cervical screening, to help make their appointments more comfortable and accessible,’ she says. ‘Self-testing which can be done at home will be a step-change for many. We have the incredible opportunity to see the back of cervical cancer. How brilliant would that be? But to achieve this, we need to support everyone eligible to attend screening.’ What if you’re anxious about cervical screening? There are plenty of completely understandable reasons someone might struggle to attend cervical screening, including embarrassment, fear of pain, lack of time or difficulties getting an appointment. ‘Women and people with a cervix who have a physical or learning disability, who are carers and struggle to find the time, people without flexible and understanding workplaces, survivors of sexual trauma or FGM, trans and non-binary people, and many more may find screening difficult to attend, painful or even traumatic,’ says Hyndman. For some, being able to take a sample privately at home and at a convenient time may make screening considerably more accessible. ‘These kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test,’ says Dr Mann. ‘It’s a simple swab you can do at home in minutes.’ Do you still need cervical screening if you've had the HPV vaccine? Yes. The HPV vaccine has had a major impact on cervical cancer rates. The first study looking at deaths prevented by the vaccine estimated that it reduced the risk of dying from cervical cancer before the age of 30 to effectively zero among vaccinated women. And, as reported by Cancer Research UK, during the five years from 2020 to 2024, no women in their early 20s died from cervical cancer in England for the first time on record. Around nine in 10 women in this age group received the HPV vaccine, most at the age of 12 or 13. However, the vaccine doesn't protect against every type of HPV that can cause cervical cancer. So even if you've been vaccinated, it's still important to take up cervical screening when invited. What symptoms should you not wait for screening to investigate? Cervical screening is designed for people who don't have symptoms. If you do notice symptoms, don't wait for a screening invitation or home test – book an appointment with your GP. According to Cancer Research UK, symptoms that should be checked include: - bleeding after sex - bleeding between periods - bleeding after menopause - unusual vaginal discharge - pelvic pain or pain during sex These symptoms can have many causes and don't automatically mean you have cervical cancer, but they should still be investigated. The bottom line The introduction of HPV self-testing is an important new option for women who haven't attended previous cervical screening appointments – but it doesn't replace clinician-led screening for those already attending routinely. ‘If you’ve been invited for cervical screening, it’s still important to attend. HPV self-testing is a new option specifically for people who have not attended previous screening appointments – it is not a replacement for clinician-led screening,’ says Hyndman. If you're invited to take part in HPV self-testing, you can order your free kit through the NHS App or your NHS online account. Your invitation will also explain any alternative ways to order. And if you're overdue but haven't received an invitation for a self-test, you can still book a cervical screening appointment at any time – even if your original invitation arrived months or years ago. For more advice, visit The Eve Appeal’s cervical screening tips. content_title: Indonesia's expanded HPV vaccine scheme ignites online falsehoods
content: Vaccine opponents have seized on Indonesia's expanded HPV inoculation programme in August, baselessly asserting the jabs are "useless" in preventing cervical cancer while repeating falsehoods the injection causes infertility. The posts cite a former health minister's criticism of the programme -- allegations that experts told AFP contradict decades of global data supporting the vaccine's safety and effectiveness. "Cervical cancer usually affects women when they're over 50 years old. Why should the vaccine be given at age 12?" Siti Fadilah Supari says in a clip shared by an Instagram user on August 8, 2026. The jabs are "useless", the former health agency head asserts, as "only about five percent" of people who get infected with HPV go on to develop cervical cancer. She also criticises the Southeast Asian archipelago's vaccination programme that was expanded in August to include schoolboys in select cities, saying it is replete with "medical irregularities" ( archived link ). "Why should boys get the HPV vaccine if they don't have a uterus?" One "major risk" of the jab is recipients having difficulty conceiving, adds the former official, who has previously made false claims about dengue and Covid-19 vaccines. Screenshot of the false post captured on August 18, 2026, with red X mark added by AFP Siti made the remarks in a video published by Biotek Farmasi Indonesia -- a company that sells herbal products online and which frequently shares other online "health education" clips featuring her. Similar claims also surfaced on Facebook , TikTok and X , ignoring the overwhelming evidence supporting HPV vaccination. AFP separately reached out to Siti and Biotek Farmasi Indonesia, but responses were not forthcoming. 'Very safe' "The HPV vaccines are very safe," Diane M. Harper , professor of obstetrics and gynaecology at the University of Michigan Medical School, told AFP on August 14. "Hundreds of millions of doses have been given, and what we see is that cervical cancer incidence is dropping," she said. "The HPV vaccines do NOT affect fertility in any way." In an email to AFP on August 19, the University of Minnesota's Vaccine Integrity Project said a review conducted in May of 121 studies found "no association between HPV vaccination and serious adverse events, including premature ovarian failure and infertility" ( archived link ). According to a World Health Organization (WHO) paper in December 2022, over 500 million doses have been distributed since the HPV vaccine's licensure in 2006 ( archived link ). "Data from all sources continue to be reassuring regarding the safety profile of HPV vaccines currently in global use," it says. The vaccine has also been proven "highly efficacious" in preventing infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The virus spreads through sexual activity, including non-penetrative sex, and affects almost everyone in their lifetime. Persistent infection with some strains causes cervical cancer in most cases. Inoculating children Because HPV is sexually transmitted, vaccination before the start of sexual activity provides the best protection, experts said. "The vaccine is only effective at preventing infection (and its consequences) before infection," Ian Frazer , emeritus professor of medicine at the University of Queensland and co-inventor of the technology enabling the HPV vaccines, told AFP on August 14 ( archived link ). Information on human papillomavirus (HPV) that causes cervical cancer. John SAEKIAdrian LEUNGAFP Both girls and boys can develop cancers from HPV when they become older, said Karin Sundström , a cancer epidemiologist at Sweden's Karolinska Institutet ( archived link ). "Cervical cancer is most famous because it is so common. But men can also die from oral, anal and penile HPV-related cancers, for example," she told AFP on August 14. "Therefore, they should also be protected from cancer." HPV can also cause throat cancer in men, said W. Martin Kast , an immunology professor at the University of Southern California ( archived link ). "Throat cancers are much more prevalent in men than women," he told AFP on August 15. "Which implies that boys would majorly benefit from getting the HPV vaccine." Sundström said the figure cited by Siti of the proportion of people who get infected with HPV and later develop cervical cancer -- five percent -- "might be correct". But that still represents "huge numbers" of people globally. "Each year, around the world more than 600,000 women are afflicted with cervical cancer, and more than 350,000 die each year from a disease, which could be prevented through timely vaccination," Sundström explained. According to data from the World Cancer Research Fund, Indonesia recorded 36,964 cervical cancer cases in 2022, putting it third after China and India in the number of cases ( archived link ). In the same year, Indonesia recorded 20,708 cervical cancer-related deaths. Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin said Indonesia will start vaccinating 11-year-old boys across the archipelago starting 2027, following its campaign in the cities of Jakarta, Bali and Yogyakarta ( archived link ). The jabs were previously only given to young Indonesian girls ( archived link ). More of our reporting on vaccine misinformation can be found here

Ask complex medical questions and find the latest clinical guidance for drugs & conditions with Medscape AI× EN RegisterLog In AI Mode Medscape Medical NewsFeatures How Strong Is Antioxidants’ Link to Cervical Cancer Risk? Tara Haelle August 25, 2026 1 6 Add to Email Alerts Jump to Key Points People who eat a diet rich in antioxidants appear to have a modestly lower risk of developing cervical cancer, a recent study showed. Based on an index assessing dietary intake of six antioxidants, each 1-unit increase in the index was linked to an 11.4% lower prevalence of cervical cancer. When the authors assessed the risk across various subgroups based on demographics or certain health status indicators, the association remained. But closer examination of the study’s methods showed substantial weaknesses, such as insufficient control for confounding, a small population, and a cross-sectional design. Antioxidants’ Role in Countering Inflammation The rationale behind investigating a link between antioxidants and cervical cancer has to do with antioxidants’ role in countering inflammation, which can slow the process of clearing a human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. “Recent review evidence suggests that protective dietary factors may influence HPV infection and cervical cancer development by modulating immune responses, oxidative stress, and inflammation,” Maozhu Lang, of the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College in Beijing, China, and colleagues wrote in the International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics. SUGGESTED FOR YOU That the underlying mechanism is immune modulation “is a solid hypothesis,” Mitchell Clark, MD, MPH, told Medscape Medical News. But they’re taking their hypothesis a step ahead of what the data can necessarily show. After referencing previous research, the authors suggest “maybe there’s something about the diet that prevents the conversion [from HPV infection] to cervical cancer. That’s a very big stretch,” continued Clark, who is an assistant professor of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive sciences at Yale School of Medicine in New Haven, Connecticut. How Dietary Intake Was Measured The researchers analyzed data from two nonconsecutive 24-hour dietary recalls, one during an in-person interview and one by phone 3-10 days later. They then calculated a Composite Dietary Antioxidant Index (CDAI) for each of six nutrients: zinc; selenium; carotenoids; and vitamins A, C, and E. The CDAI is a unit-less statistic that subtracts the mean population intake of each nutrient from each participant’s mean intake based on the two daily intake recalls and then divides that difference by the standard deviation. Since the CDAI is a population-based ratio, it does not correlate to an actual amount of antioxidant intake. Study Limitations The findings come from a retrospective, cross-sectional, observational study with participants in eight cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES; 2003-2018). NHANES is a nationally representative survey conducted by the CDC that adequately represents the US population. While the survey had an initial 80,312 participants, this study’s final population was 1044 people after exclusions for missing data. The study matched 174 people with self-reported cervical cancer to 870 control participants by demographic characteristics, education, household income, BMI, and marital, smoking, alcohol consumption, hypertension, and diabetes status. After adjustment for those covariates, they identified less prevalence of cervical cancer for each 1-unit increase in the CDAI (odds ratio, 0.886; P = .003). “It’s a very small population, and we don’t have a lot of information about the characteristics of the people included,” said Clark, commenting on the study. An observational study also cannot offer any insight into causality, but cross-sectional studies are particularly limiting since data from a one-time survey provides only a single snapshot in time of participants’ diet, behavior, and cancer status. Nearly all cervical cancer cases are caused by HPV, and it can take 15-20 years before an HPV infection subsequently develops into cervical dysplasia or cancer. “With this cancer in particular and that long timeline, there are so many things that happen along the way that may influence someone’s ability to clear the infection earlier — meaning they are less likely to get cervical cancer — or environmental and health factors that are contributing to persistent infection and increased risk of high-grade dysplasia and progression to cervical cancer,” Clark said. A snapshot in time with two 24-hour dietary recalls rarely accurately represents longitudinal dietary habits. Even smoking status collected at one point in time may not reflect a person’s lifetime smoking status, he continued. Others limitations to using 24-hour dietary recalls is that they are subject to recall bias and social desirability bias, potentially exaggerating, minimizing, or omitting certain foods. The researchers considered multiple covariates associated with risk for cancer but plenty of information is missing that makes it hard to assess a real association between antioxidant intake and the risk for cervical cancer, Clark said. These include HPV vaccination status, history of cervical cancer screenings or their adherence to screening recommendations, history of cervical dysplasia, history of HPV infection or any HPV-related malignancies, and whether a participant had an autoimmune condition or was taking any immunosuppressing medications. “Chronic steroid use, patients who are immunocompromised due to HIV, patients who may be using methotrexate or have rheumatoid arthritis — all of those are things we know inhibit the immune system,” which affects HPV status and the ability of the body to clear HPV, Clark continued. “The whole crux of the problem here is that HPV is so prevalent in the community,” he explained. “Most reproductive age adults will be exposed to HPV at some point in their life, and the vast majority of them will clear the virus with natural immunity that they develop to the virus or through vaccination long before the HPV has an opportunity to integrate into the cells of the lower genital tract or the head and neck and begin oncogenic transformation into a malignancy.” Further, while age was a covariate included by the authors, the actual ages of the participants were not provided. “We would need to know the proportion of younger people and whether they were evenly distributed between young, middle, and older patients,” Clark said. “We know that younger patients are far more likely to clear their HPV infections spontaneously compared to older people, and in older people who have persistent HPV, the longer it is persistent, the more likely they are to progress into a cervical cancer.” Antioxidant Intake’s Potential Link to Overall Health The study cannot assess health-seeking behaviors or other health behaviors that might be associated with both antioxidant intake and risk for cervical cancer. It’s possible, Clark said, that dietary status in general reflects overall better access to health. “Are we just perhaps capturing a group of people who are better connected to health literacy and access to preventive care,” Clark said, “because we know the majority of cervical cancers are in patients who do not adhere to screening guidelines.” Although the authors included education and income level, they are not strong enough proxies alone to account for differences in overall lifestyles or access to HPV vaccination or cervical cancer screening. In considering access to ob/gyn and family medicine in rural areas, for example, there may be significant overlaps between health deserts and food deserts, Clark said. The study did not include geographic location or participants’ urbanicity as covariates. Broadly speaking, more robust studies that consider long-term dietary patterns and lifestyle factors would be necessary, likely paired with in vitro or animal model mechanistic studies, to better characterize what role antioxidants might play in cervical cancer risk. Improving access to HPV vaccination and cervical cancer screenings would also have a bigger impact on risk reduction, Clark said, and may be easier to implement than behavioral dietary changes. The research was funded by the National Key Clinical Specialty Construction Project. The authors reported no conflicts of interest. Clark reported consulting for AbbVie. LetsGetChecked Powered by Fuze Health Partners with Waters Corporation to Bring the Most Comprehensive FDA-Cleared At-Home HPV Cervical Cancer Screening Tool Available in the U.S. Today to Patients LetsGetChecked powered by Fuze Health today announced it now offers the most comprehensive FDA-cleared at-home HPV screening tool available in the U.S. today. Business Wire Thu, August 27, 2026 at 7:00 AM PDT 4 min read New FDA-cleared offering expands access to evidence-based cervical cancer screening through LetsGetChecked's end-to-end care experience WEST CHESTER, Ohio, August 27, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--LetsGetChecked powered by Fuze Health today announced it now offers the OnclarityTM HPV Self-Collection Kit, tested with the BD OnclarityTM HPV Assay, the most comprehensive FDA-cleared at-home HPV screening tool available in the U.S. today. This offering underscores LetsGetChecked's commitment to expanding patient access to evidence-based screening solutions. According to the National Cancer Institute (NCI), roughly one in four women in the U.S. are not up to date with cervical cancer screening, and about half of women diagnosed with cervical cancer had either never been screened or were overdue.1 At-home self-collection has the potential to help close this significant screening gap by addressing key barriers to cervical cancer screening. These include concerns about the screening experience, logistical challenges, socioeconomic factors, prior sexual trauma, and limited awareness of available screening options.2,3,4 LetsGetChecked's expertise in at-home sample collection, design, and patient engagement was instrumental in developing a self-collection experience that is accessible, intuitive, and advances women's health. The launch expands on LetsGetChecked's 2023 FDA De Novo authorization—the first-ever granted for an at-home chlamydia and gonorrhea sample collection system—and reflects more than 13 years of experience delivering at-home screening programs.5 Expanding access to evidence-based cervical cancer screening advances Fuze Health's commitment to shift women's healthcare from reactive treatment to earlier detection and prevention. This is supported by a seamless experience that brings together preventive screening, laboratory testing, personalized treatment support, and ongoing care. "Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers, yet millions of women remain unscreened because traditional models of care don't work for everyone," said Oonagh O'Brien, Chief Executive Officer of LetsGetChecked. "By expanding our women's health offerings with an at-home HPV testing solution, we're making it easier for our partners to deliver evidence-based preventive care and giving individuals high-quality screening on their own terms." The OnclarityTM HPV Self-Collection Kit is tested with the BD OnclarityTM HPV Assay, which detects 14 high-risk HPV genotypes to identify oncogenic risk and is the only FDA-approved HPV assay to identify six individual genotypes and three groups of pooled results, making it the most comprehensive HPV screening tool available in the U.S. today. Results from the extended genotyping can enable timely referral to a specialist in high-risk cases and avoid unnecessary follow-up testing in lower-risk patients.6 Story Continues "Reaching the millions of women and persons with a cervix who remain unscreened or under-screened for cervical cancer will require new thinking and innovative approaches," said Jane Montealegre, PhD, Associate Professor, Behavioral Science, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, TX. "At-home HPV screening represents a major opportunity to reach women through transformative solutions, helping expand access to care and bringing us closer to the goal of eliminating cervical cancer." content: Nearly a third of women aged 21 to 29 have never been screened for cervical cancer , according to research tracking screening trends over 20 years. The proportion of women in their 20s who reported never being screened for cervical cancer has increased over the past two decades. Among women aged 30 to 64, almost 15 per cent also reported never having been screened. Researchers at MUSC Hollings Cancer Center analysed self-reported data from the National Health Interview Survey to examine the proportion of women who said they had never received screening in their lifetime. Cervical screening aims to detect precancer and early-stage cancer, when treatment can be easier. Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination is the first line of defence against cervical cancer, with regular screening the next. First author Kalyani Sonawane, assistant director for data science and analytics at Hollings, said: “A lot of times national surveys look at the up-to-date rate, meaning how many women are up to date on their screening. “But this paper is slightly different because it measures the proportion of women who reported that in their lifetime, they’ve never received screening.” Because the data was self-reported, the researchers said some women may have misremembered whether they had previously been screened. The proportion of women who had never been screened increased by 5 per cent each year, while diagnoses of regional- and distant-stage cervical cancer also increased among women aged 30 to 64. The researchers said lower screening rates could potentially contribute to cancers being detected after they have spread, once a woman notices symptoms and goes to the doctor, but the study was not designed to determine whether the two trends were linked. The findings also showed that 45 per cent of women in their 20s were not vaccinated against HPV. Sonawane said the researchers were unsure why the proportion of women who had never been screened was increasing. In previous unpublished work, the team examined women’s responses about why they had not been screened. Many reported having no particular reason or said their healthcare provider had not raised screening with them. Sonawane also suggested some women vaccinated against HPV might believe they no longer need screening, although screening guidelines continue to recommend it after vaccination. The research found further disparities, with uninsured women, women living in the South and racial minorities particularly likely to report that they had never been screened. Absolutely. Here is what every man should know Published 2 weeks ago on August 13, 2026 By News Desk By Ruby Raut, founder, WUKA Every time we post a dad talking to his daughter about periods, the internet seems to split in two. One side says: “This is brilliant. I wish my dad had spoken to me like this.” The other says: “Why on earth are men talking about periods?” And I always find that second reaction fascinating. Because men might not menstruate, but they live in a world with people who do. Your daughter might get her first period while you are the only parent at home. Your teenage niece might bleed through her clothes while you are driving her somewhere. Your girlfriend might wake up at 3am with cramps. Your wife might suddenly realise she has run out of period products . A colleague might bleed through her trousers during a meeting. A girl you coach might quietly tell you she cannot play because she has started her period. At some point in your life, there is a very good chance a woman or girl will have a period around you. And at that moment, you have two options. You can be calm, informed and useful. Or you can stand there looking as if nobody ever taught you what a period actually involves. So perhaps we need a Haynes manual for men and periods. Not a biology degree or a lecture.Just the information every man should probably know. First: yes, men should know what a period actually is Let us start with the basics. A period is not simply “a bit of blood once a month”. Menstruation is part of the menstrual cycle . The lining of the uterus builds up and, if there is no pregnancy , that lining is shed. That is the bleeding part. But for many women and girls, the experience can also involve cramps, back pain, headaches, bloating, tiredness, diarrhoea, tender breasts, mood changes and generally feeling pretty rotten. Some barely notice their period. Others are completely floored by it. This is important because one of the least helpful things you can say to somebody struggling with their period is: “Is it really that bad?” You do not need to experience period pain to believe someone when they tell you they are in pain. Second: if a girl tells you she has started her period, do not panic This one is particularly important for dads. Imagine your daughter gets her first period while Mum is out. What does she need from you? Probably not a horrified expression or you shouting across the house, “YOUR PERIOD HAS STARTED!” She needs you to behave as though this is an entirely normal bodily function. Because it is. Ask her what she needs. Find her a period product. If there is blood on her clothes, help her sort it out without making a huge fuss. If she does not know how to use a pad or period underwear, help her find clear instructions. And please do not make jokes about her “becoming a woman”. For a young girl, a first period can already feel confusing, embarrassing and frightening. Your job is not to make it into a ceremony but to make her feel safe. Sometimes the most useful sentence a dad can say is simply: “Okay. No problem. What do you need?” Third: learn what period products actually are Pads.Tampons.Period underwear.Menstrual cups.Period swimwear. You do not have to develop strong opinions about all of them. You just need to know they exist. If someone asks you to buy pads, do not behave as though you have been sent into a nuclear reactor without protective clothing. Go to the period aisle. Text them a photo if you are unsure. Ask which absorbency they want. Buy the product. Come home. And if you are the father of a daughter, having a few period products in the bathroom before she starts menstruating is a very sensible idea. You keep toilet roll in your house before somebody needs it. Period products should not feel radically different. Fourth: never announce a period stain This should be basic human etiquette. If you notice that a woman or girl has bled through her clothes, tell her quietly and discreetly. Do not point, laugh, or whisper about it to someone else. And definitely never announce it to the room. If you have a jumper or jacket she can tie around her waist, offer it. If there is somewhere she can clean up or change, help her get there. Then move on with your life. Period leaks happen. The embarrassment surrounding them is often far worse than the actual blood. Fifth: stop using periods as an explanation for every emotion “Are you on your period?” Four words capable of making almost any disagreement significantly worse. Sometimes a woman is angry because she is angry and sometimes she disagrees with you because she disagrees with you. Sometimes you genuinely are being annoying. Hormonal changes can affect mood for some people, but using menstruation to dismiss a woman’s feelings is patronising and incredibly unhelpful. If your partner says she feels emotional before her period, listen to her. That does not permit you to diagnose every future disagreement as PMS. Sixth: period pain is not something every woman should simply put up with There is an extraordinary tendency to tell girls from a young age that painful periods are just part of being female. For some, mild cramps are manageable. For others, period pain can be severe enough to disrupt school, work, sleep, exercise and everyday life. So if your daughter is doubled over in pain every month, repeatedly missing school, fainting, vomiting or unable to function normally, do not tell her to toughen up. Take her seriously and help her seek medical advice. Being a supportive dad does not require you to know what is causing her symptoms. It requires you to believe her when she says something is wrong. Seventh: men talking about periods does not take anything away from women This is perhaps the strangest objection to our Dads and Periods campaign. The idea that periods somehow belong in a conversation that only women are allowed to have. Women should absolutely lead conversations about their own bodies and experiences. But understanding periods should not be restricted to people who menstruate. We teach children about digestion even though they are not gastroenterologists and about first aid even though most people are not doctors. We teach boys about pregnancy even though they will never be pregnant. Knowledge is not ownership. A father understanding periods does not make periods less female. It makes him a better prepared father. A boy understanding periods does not mean he suddenly understands exactly what menstruation feels like. It means he is less likely to laugh when a girl gets a stain on her skirt. A male coach understanding periods does not make him an expert on women’s bodies. It means a teenage player might feel able to tell him why she needs five minutes off the pitch instead of inventing an excuse. A male partner understanding periods does not mean he has to track every detail of his girlfriend’s cycle. It might simply mean that when she says, “My cramps are awful today,” his response is not, “Again?” So should men talk about periods? Yes. But perhaps “talk” is not even the most important word. Men should know about periods. Men should be comfortable hearing about periods. Men should know what to do when someone starts one unexpectedly. Men should know how to buy period products. Men should know not to make somebody feel ashamed about bleeding. And fathers, in particular, should be able to talk about periods with their daughters without embarrassment. Because there is a bigger point here. Girls learn very quickly which subjects make adults uncomfortable. If Dad goes silent every time periods are mentioned, she notices. If he leaves every period conversation to Mum, she notices. If he wrinkles his nose at period products, she notices. And she may quietly absorb the message that this part of her body is something men find disgusting or embarrassing. That is exactly the message we should be trying to dismantle. At WUKA, we started our Dads and Periods campaign because we want fathers to feel capable of having these conversations. Not perfectly. Not scientifically. Not with a PowerPoint presentation about the uterus over Sunday lunch. Just normally. Periods happen. Roughly half the population will experience them at some point in their lives. The other half should probably know what they are. And if the choice is between a dad who knows what a period is, knows where the period products are kept and can calmly help his daughter when she needs him, or a dad hovering helplessly outside the bathroom shouting, “SHALL I CALL YOUR MUM?” I know which one I would rather have. Millions of lives saved. One revolutionary vaccine Feature 20 years. Millions of lives saved. One revolutionary vaccine 28 August 2026 It's been 20 years since the first doses of the HPV vaccine were administred in 2006 (top right). The vaccine was created by Emeritus Professor Ian Frazer AC (foreground and top left) and his colleague Dr Jian Zhou (bottom left). (Photo credit: © The University of Queensland. Courtesy of the University Archives ) Twenty years ago, the first dose of a UQ-developed vaccine was given to a teenage girl in Brisbane. That same vaccine is now on track to end cervical cancer in Australia. August 28, 2026, marks the 20th anniversary of the first dose of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine – now known as Gardasil 9 – which immunises recipients against the virus that is the leading cause of cervical cancer. The vaccine, developed by Emeritus Professor Ian Frazer AC and the late Dr Jian Zhou, is now offered to all children aged 12-13 years old through the school-based National Immunisation Program. Worldwide, more than 600 million doses of Gardasil have been administered. Professor Frazer, who is now retired from UQ and serves on the board of the Translational Research Institute (TRI) Foundation, said ridding Australia of cervical cancer was a result he’d only dreamed of when he started looking into HPV in the 1980s. “We couldn’t have imagined the impact this research would have and I feel very privileged to have been a part of this outcome,” Professor Frazer said. 1/7 Professor Ian Frazer. 2/7 Professor Ian Frazer (bottom right) and colleagues in the early 1990s. (Photo credit: © The University of Queensland. Courtesy of the University Archives ) 3/7 Professor Ian Frazer in the mid-1990s. (Photo credit: © The University of Queensland. Courtesy of the University Archives ) 4/7 Dr Jian Zhou. 5/7 Emma McMillan after receiving her HPV vaccine in 2006. 6/7 Professor Ian Frazer and Dr Jian Zhou accept the European Inventor Award in 2015. 7/7 Professor Ian Frazer at UQ. Previous Next Creating the legacy Professor Frazer met Dr Zhou in 1989 while on sabbatical at the University of Cambridge, where Dr Zhou was a research fellow. After realising they shared a research interest in HPV, Professor Frazer invited Dr Zhou and his wife, fellow researcher Dr Xiao Yi Sun, to work at UQ. For a year they worked on replicating the virus, and then in 1991 they were working in the lab and noticed virus-like particles on an electron micrograph – an image captured using an electron microscope. “Jian said, ‘We’ve got the shell of the virus’ and I said, ‘Yes, and we’ve probably got a vaccine’,” Professor Frazer said. “We knew that because we got something that looked like the virus, there was a good chance that it could be a vaccine.” They filed the first patent and in 1994, UQ’s commercial arm UniQuest licenced the intellectual property to CSL Limited in Melbourne, which then sub-licensed the HPV technology to Merck & Co 2 years later to start developing a vaccine. The vaccine was ready for clinical trials in 1997, with testing continuing for 8 years. However, the legacy took a heartbreaking turn in 1999 when Dr Zhou died after a brief illness. Professor Ian Frazer with Dr Jian Zhou's widow and fellow researcher Dr Xiao Yi Sun. “It’s sad that Jian died before the work was publicly recognised,” Professor Frazer said. “It’s important we recognise his major contribution to everything that was achieved.” Dr Sun, who was part of the research team, said it was overwhelming to think about the impact of the research. “Were he alive today, Jian would simply be grateful that his work has helped save lives because that was his nature” Dr Sun said. “Were he alive today, Jian would simply be grateful that his work has helped save lives because that was his nature” Dr Sun said. “He always approached science with humility, creative thinking, and a determination to do the very best work he could for the benefit of others.” Phase 3 clinical trials involved more than 12,000 women and girls aged 16-26, across 13 countries. The clinical evidence was so strong that the study was halted early to enable the young women in the placebo group to receive the vaccine. Women who received first dose remember the significance Following international and national drug approvals, history was made on 28 August 2006 when the first official dose of the Gardasil vaccine was given to teenage girls at the Princess Alexandra Hospital in Brisbane. Rachel Kerr (nee McMillan) was 15 years old at the time, and her parents Nigel and Denise McMillan, were colleagues of Professor Frazer. “I remember the day as being important and that vaccines were obviously good things that help people,” Ms Kerr recalled. “I was more nervous about the cameras on the day, not so much the needle. But I do remember they gave us a lollipop at the end!” Now, as a mother of 2 and a paediatric nurse, Ms Kerr can see how vital vaccines are. Sisters Emma Sciacca and Rachel Kerr received the first doses of the HPV vaccine as teenagers in 2006. (Photo credit: Inset images: © The University of Queensland. Courtesy of the University Archives) “They are obviously really important from a public health perspective,” she said. “I have seen reports that cervical cancer is on its way to being eliminated in young women in Australia, and it is just so amazing that has been able to happen. “Hopefully by the time my children grow up, no women in their cohort will get cervical cancer.” “Hopefully by the time my children grow up, no women in their cohort will get cervical cancer.” Rachel’s younger sister, veterinarian Dr Emma Sciacca, is also proud to have been part of a such a significant health breakthrough. “I am very grateful for the protection the vaccine has given me against an awful disease and, as an adult and parent to 3 children, I’d make the same decision,” Dr Sciacca said. “With both our parents being scientists, I recall there was a lot of excitement about the vaccine and what had been achieved.” Eliminating cervical cancer Studies have shown that because of the vaccine, Australia is on track to become the first country to eliminate cervical cancer by 2035. The 2025 Cervical Cancer Elimination Progress Report stated there were no new cervical cancer cases diagnosed in women aged under 25 years in 2021. “This remarkable achievement is almost certainly due to the impact of HPV vaccination,” the report stated. UQ’s Vice-Chancellor and President, Professor Deborah Terry AC said the Gardasil vaccine had been revolutionary in many ways. “It was the first vaccine in the world to protect against any kind of cancer and has been the impetus for the strong biomedical sector we have in Queensland today,” Professor Terry said. “There is no better example of the role research universities play in solving some of society’s greatest challenges. “Professor Frazer and Dr Zhou’s tenacity has also made an immense difference to people’s lives at home and abroad. “Great scientists are more than just curious. “They have an awareness of the impact of their curiosity and how they can channel it to not only to pursue scientific breakthroughs, but to realise the benefits of their work for humanity and for society more broadly.” Dr Xiao Yi Sun with her son Andreas Zhou (left) visit a UQ lab. Worldwide impact Figures show cervical cancer vaccines, like Gardasil, have saved millions of lives across the world. But Professor Frazer cautions there is still a long way to go. “The cervical cancer vaccine has been well used in the developed world, but we still have a major problem getting the vaccine into the developing world, where screening programs are also limited,” Professor Frazer said. “This is where I hope the future focus will be.” Dr Sun agrees. “Seeing Australia move towards eliminating cervical cancer is deeply encouraging and my hope is that this life-saving vaccine continues to reach those who need it most,’’ Dr Sun said. “I have always admired Professor Frazer’s dedication over many years to helping people in developing countries benefit from the HPV vaccine. “I hope we can continue working towards making this protection available to everyone who needs it.” Epidemiologist and one of the scientists that co-led the World Health Organization Cervical Cancer Elimination Modelling Consortium, Professor Karen Canfell AC, from the Cancer Elimination Collaboration at the University of Sydney, said HPV vaccines have opened the door to a new ‘elimination’ framework for addressing the global cancer burden. “Aspiring to eliminate any disease is profound, let alone having an evidence-based global strategy, with targets, to guide its achievement,” Professor Canfell said. “A generation ago, it’s difficult to imagine anyone discussing disease elimination and cancer in the same sentence. “A generation ago, it’s difficult to imagine anyone discussing disease elimination and cancer in the same sentence. “It’s a wonderful legacy, and a great time to celebrate the remarkable achievements of Ian Frazer, Jian Zhou and their team.” What’s next? Cervical cancer was estimated to cause around 340,000 deaths in women worldwide in 2022, and it leaves more than 200,000 children without a mother every year. Professor Canfell said while Australia is on track for elimination by 2035, further efforts and investment will be required to realise elimination equitably. “On current trends, it will take First Nations Australians over a decade longer to attain the elimination goal,” Professor Canfell said. “Addressing inequities is the top priority, and there needs to be a concerted effort to reach all unvaccinated girls and boys and all eligible unscreened and under-screened adults. “It’s a matter of saving as many lives as possible in the short term, while building the core and having a sustainable plan to ensure the long-term elimination goals will also be met.’’ Professor Ian Frazer in UQ's Great Court. Can we vaccinate against other cancers? WHO data shows cancer-causing infections are responsible for about 30 per cent of cancers in low-and middle-income countries, and 10 per cent worldwide. Known cancer-causing infections include some strains of papillomavirus, hepatitis viruses (B and C), the glandular fever virus Epstein Barr, and some polyoma viruses. HPV is responsible for almost all cervical cancers, as well as several perineal, genitoanal and oral cancers. Professor Frazer said vaccines for other viruses that cause cancer are possible. “We already have effective vaccines to prevent infection with some viruses,” Professor Frazer said. “Vaccines against hepatitis B and papillomavirus, for instance, have reduced the burden of cancer caused by these viruses. “We know how to do the work. All it will take is funding to support the research, scientists working on these vaccines, and time. “Research and science are always a joint venture.” Topics Health and medicine Share Related articles UQ Medical Program to expand from major funding boost The University of Queensland will offer 10 additional places for domestic students to train as doctors in regional and rural communities, as part of a Federal Government initiative to strengthen the GP and rural medical workforce. 28 August 2026 Analysis Twenty years on, the Gardasil story is still being written August marks 20 years since the first dose of Gardasil® was administered, beginning a new chapter in the prevention of cervical cancer. 28 August 2026 Media contact UQ Communications communications@uq.edu.au +61 429 056 139 Subscribe to UQ News Get the latest from our newsroom

They also offer a discreet alternative that can be done at home. How the home test works The HPV self-testing kit contains a swab, similar to a long cotton bud, which is used to collect a sample from the vagina. You can then post the sample back to the NHS free of charge, where it will be tested for high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV). HPV is a common virus that can cause changes in cervical cells. Some types of HPV can increase the risk of cervical cancer, but detecting the virus through screening can help identify people who may need further checks before cancer develops. If high-risk HPV is detected, the person will be invited to attend a follow-up cervical screening appointment at their GP surgery or a sexual health clinic. A healthcare professional will then take a sample directly from the cervix to check for abnormal cell changes. Who will be offered the kits? The HPV self-testing kit is being introduced in phases across England. The first people to receive invitations will be aged between 30 and 65 and will not have attended cervical screening after previous NHS invitations. Invitations will be sent through the NHS App, text message, email or letter. Those invited can order a free kit through the NHS App or their NHS online account. The NHS hopes the new approach will help address barriers that prevent people from attending screening appointments, including embarrassment, lack of time and concerns about discomfort. The importance of screening Although self-testing is being introduced as an additional option, NHS cervical screening appointments with a clinician remain the preferred method of screening for those who routinely attend. The latest figures show that 68.8% of eligible women in England are currently up to date with cervical screening, below the NHS England target of 80%. Around four million women are therefore not up to date. The NHS is offering cervical screening to eligible women aged 24 to 64, with invitations generally sent every five years unless more frequent monitoring is required. Women who have previously received an invitation can still arrange an appointment, even if the invitation was sent months or years ago. Part of the 2040 elimination target The rollout follows the YouScreen trial carried out in North London in 2021. The trial found that offering HPV self-testing to women who were not up to date with screening could significantly increase participation, potentially resulting in around 400,000 additional women being screened each year in England. The UK National Screening Committee later used evidence from the trial to recommend wider implementation. The HPV self-testing kits are part of the NHS’s ambition to eliminate cervical cancer in England by 2040, alongside efforts to increase HPV vaccination and improve participation in cervical screening. Women who receive an invitation are encouraged to take up the offer, whether through the new home-testing option or a traditional screening appointment. Even those who have received the HPV vaccine should continue with screening, as the vaccine does not protect against every type of HPV that can cause cervical cancer. content: Thank you for registering Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in Jump to content Open full menu US Edition UK EditionAsia EditionEdición en Español Log in Log in News Sports Culture Lifestyle Money Travel Premium Climate More Swipe for next article News Health Millions of women in England to receive ‘game-changing’ at-home HPV testing kits Eligible women aged between 30 and 65 will be sent invitations through the NHS app, text message, email or by letter Copy link Bookmark 2Comments Go to comments Bookmark popover Removed from bookmarks Close popover Related: Jersey Shore star Snooki reveals cervical cancer diagnosis Free at-home testing kits are to be sent to millions of women in England on the NHS who have missed their cervical screening appointments. Described as a "gamechanger", the scheme offers a "discreet and convenient option" intended to persuade more women to undertake screening. Included in each kit is a swab, which is utilised to collect a vaginal sample. This is then returned to NHS laboratories without charge, where scientists test the sample for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV). Where high-risk HPV is found, patients will subsequently be requested to go to a clinician for a cervical screening appointment. RECOMMENDED Dolly Parton net worth: The country legend had no kids. Where is her fortune going? Ted Cruz deletes Dolly Parton tribute in latest social media disaster Squirt Some Honey On Your Dog’s Tongue, Here’s What HappensPets Daily Health | SponsoredSponsored Cesar Millan Reveals What Honey Does to Your Aging DogPets Daily Health | SponsoredSponsored HPV is a group of viruses which can be passed on through sexual contact and cause no symptoms. Even so, approximately 13 high-risk forms of the virus are known to cause 99.7% of all cervical cancer cases. Invitations started to be distributed yesterday to eligible women aged 30 to 65 who have missed appointments, arriving by letter, email, text message or the NHS app. open image in gallery The phased rollout forms part of the NHS’s target of eliminating cervical cancer by 2040 (Alamy/PA) They will then be able to order a kit through the NHS app or online. The phased rollout forms part of the NHS’s target of eliminating cervical cancer by 2040. Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women’s health at NHS England, said: “Screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier, but only around two thirds of women are attending cervical screening appointments when invited by the NHS. “Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a gamechanger – making it easier than ever for them to get tested for HPV.” Women aged between 24 and 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years, or more often if HPV is detected. Main symptoms of cervical cancer NHS Symptoms of cervical cancer include: vaginal bleeding that's unusual for you – including bleeding during or after sex, between your periods or after menopause, or having heavier periods than usual changes to your vaginal discharge pain during sex pain in your lower back, between your hip bones (pelvis), or in your lower tummy Latest figures from NHS England show 68.8% of eligible women are up to date with cervical screening, below the 80% target. The health service estimates this means around four million women are not up to date. Dr Mann said: “There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time, or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test. “So, if you’re invited to take part, please order a test – it’s a simple swab you can do at home in minutes.” Gem Sofianos-Boorman was diagnosed with cervical cancer at 28 after taking up her cervical screening invite. She said “it was the last thing” she expected, as she was “young, healthy, and had no symptoms”. Ms Sofianos-Boorman, now 39, said: “Looking back, I truly believe that going to my screening appointment saved my life. “My cancer was found early, which allowed me to have treatment before it spread. “That’s why it’s great news that the NHS is making it more accessible for some people to take part in screening. Cervical cancer often doesn’t cause symptoms in its early stages, so screening plays a really important role in finding something before it might become serious.” Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said: “Cervical cancer is preventable – but that’s why we want to make it as easy and convenient as possible for women to keep up with their screening. open image in gallery Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the NHS is ‘acting as early as possible to stop preventable deaths’ (Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA) (PA Wire) “These free self-testing kits will be offered to four million women who are currently behind on their screening to make it easier for as many women as possible to keep themselves healthy and safe. “This is the future NHS we are building – there for all of us when we need it, and acting as early as possible to stop preventable deaths.” Athena Lamnisos, chief executive at The Eve Appeal, said: “Cervical screening is designed to prevent cervical cancer rather than respond to symptoms, attending a clinic requires people to actively prioritise an appointment among the many competing demands of everyday life. “Self-testing which can be done at home will be a step-change for many. “We have the incredible opportunity to see the back of cervical cancer. How brilliant would that be? But to achieve this, we need to support everyone eligible to attend screening. “This is not a replacement for clinician screening, and we will continue to work with and support those attending their traditional cervical screening, to help make their appointments more comfortable and accessible.” Michelle Mitchell, chief executive of Cancer Research UK, said: “At-home HPV self-testing kits will help more people take part in a way that works for them. “If people receive their cervical screening or self-testing kit invitation, please consider taking up the offer and encourage loved ones to do the same. “Beating cervical cancer means beating it for everyone, and this move brings us closer to that goal.” It comes as experts responded last week to claims that suggest the brush used in cervical cancer smear tests is sterilised in a “cancer-causing” chemical.
